summary: Bellflower packs nearly 77,000 people into just 6.2 square miles — a density of over 12,400 per square mile — yet the landscape is almost perfectly flat, with no hills, canyons, or coastal views to break the grid of single-story commercial strips and tightly spaced residential blocks that define southeast Los Angeles County. That flatness and density create an unusual tension: the city functions overwhelmingly as a bedroom community, with most workers commuting outward to the logistics hubs along the I-710 corridor, healthcare systems in Long Beach and Downey, or employers scattered across greater LA, yet the street grid itself is compact enough that everyday errands — grocery runs, laundromats, taco shops, fast-casual spots along Bellflower Boulevard — sit within short drives or bike rides. The affordability math is illuminating: a median home value of $661,100 against a median household income of $77,602 yields a price-to-income ratio above 8.5, meaning ownership requires either substantial savings or dual high-earning households, while median rent at $1,771 consumes roughly 27% of gross median income — tight but within conventional thresholds. Climate is genuinely mild, averaging 76°F highs with 9.4 hours of daily sunshine year-round, and the flat terrain makes evening walks easy even if dedicated trail networks and large parks are sparse. Bellflower is, at its core, an affordable-by-LA-standards grid city where proximity to freeways is the main geographic asset, and the tradeoff for that access is a landscape shaped more by pavement than by open space.
